summary: Marble is World Labs' hosted generative world model and the product built on it: give it a sentence, one or several photographs, a 360 panorama, a short video or a coarse block-out you draw in its own modelling tool, and about five minutes later you get back a three-dimensional place you can walk around in a browser. The place is stored as several million three-dimensional Gaussian splats, which the vendor calls its highest-fidelity form, and it can also be handed over as a coarse mesh for physics, as two higher-quality meshes for drawing, as a panorama, or as a recorded video. It can be edited by describing the change, grown past its original edges, varied by changing a seed, and several worlds can be placed beside one another into a larger one. Everything else a shared world needs is absent by design: no session, no participants, no identity, no rules, no sound and no position on the Earth, which is why fifty-eight of the eighty-nine rows here are honestly out of scope. Two traps matter for a standards audience. The first is that Marble writes an open splat format in a coordinate frame that format does not expect, corrects for it in its own viewer, and describes the frame three different ways across three of its own pages - so a conforming reader gets an upside-down world. The second is that the words reconstruct, generate and simulate are used together in the vendor's own framing, while what actually ships simulates nothing: it produces a static asset for someone else's engine to run, and the vendor's own writing places interactivity in the future.

coverage.note: Marble is a hosted generative service and a web viewer, not a renderer: it publishes no pass structure, no render graph and no rasterisation rules. The renderer it names, for its own site and for everyone else, is Spark, a separate MIT-licensed library built on three.js.

coverage.note: Marble writes files in an open splat format but not in that format's frame. The format stores right-up-back by default, following the graphics and three.js convention; Marble's generated files declare a raw computer-vision frame, and Marble's own viewer corrects for it with a half-turn about the X axis before drawing. A conforming reader that follows the format therefore renders a Marble world upside down, which is exactly the question the vendor's own export page answers. Worse for a reader trying to comply, three vendor pages disagree: a release note says exports moved to the graphics frame in December 2025, the export specification page still states the computer-vision frame, and the developer page names a raw computer-vision convention for generated files.

coverage.note: World Labs publishes a REST World API (with API keys, an OpenAPI file and an llms.txt index) that generates a world from text, images or video, sets whether it is public, lists, exports and deletes worlds. It manages only API-generated worlds and has no endpoint for editing an existing world in place.

It has no extension names and no rule for a recipient that does not understand the data. Searched the 55 pages of the World Labs documentation index for extension, plugin and metadata on 2026-10-20; no other mechanism.
